title: Excel Sheet Column Number
description: Brute force to optimized: recomputing each base-26 power from scratch versus folding letters in left to right with a running shift-and-add.

blocks.text: Given a string columnTitle representing an Excel style column heading, where A is 1, B is 2, and so on up to Z being 26, then AA, AB, and onward, return the corresponding column number.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Number System With No Zero
blocks.text: This is an ordinary base 26 number system, almost identical to how digits combine in base 10, except there is no digit worth zero, the smallest digit, A, is already worth 1. That single difference is exactly what causes the sequence to go Z, then AA, rather than needing a placeholder the way base 10 rolls from 9 to 10.

blocks.caption: Each letter has a value from 1 to 26, weighted by its position like a base 26 number

blocks.text: This looks like a brand new kind of math problem, but it is worth checking how closely it matches the shift-and-rebuild idea already used for peeling and reconstructing digits in Reverse Integer.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Computing 26 raised to a position's power from scratch every single time repeats an enormous amount of multiplication that was already implicit in the calculation for the position right before it.

Observation 2: Reading the title from left to right instead of right to left changes the shape of the problem entirely, each new letter can be folded directly into a running result by multiplying the existing result by 26, then adding the new letter's value, the exact same shift-and-add idea used to read an ordinary base 10 number, or to rebuild a value one digit at a time as in Reverse Integer.

Observation 3: Testing this against "AB" confirms it, reading A first gives a running result of 1, then folding in B gives 1 times 26 plus 2, which is 28, matching the position-weighted calculation directly.

Observation 4: The one genuine wrinkle this number system has that base 10 does not is that there is no digit worth zero, A is already worth 1, which is exactly why the sequence rolls from Z straight into AA, instead of needing a placeholder the way base 10 rolls from 9 into 10.

Naming this explicitly as a base conversion, with a shift-and-add left to right scan and one missing zero digit, turns an unfamiliar Excel quirk into a direct application of a technique already understood.

Read the title from right to left. For every position, compute how much that position is worth, 26 raised to the power of its distance from the rightmost character, by multiplying 26 by itself that many times from scratch, then multiply by the letter's own value and add it to a running total.

items: Loop over every position i, counting from the rightmost character of the title, starting at 0.
Find the value of the letter at that position, A is 1, B is 2, and so on.
Compute 26 raised to the power of i by multiplying 26 by itself i times.
Multiply the letter's value by that power, and add it to a running total.

blocks.caption: Brute force flow: recompute the base 26 power from scratch for every position

codes.python:
def title_to_number(column_title):
    n = len(column_title)
    total = 0
    for i in range(n):                            # i counts positions from the right, starting at 0
        letter_value = ord(column_title[n - 1 - i]) - ord('A') + 1
        power = 1
        for _ in range(i):
            power *= 26                              # recompute 26 to the power of i from scratch
        total += letter_value * power
    return total


if __name__ == "__main__":
    column_title = "ZY"
    print(title_to_number(column_title))

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The outer loop counts positions from the right, starting at 0, so that the exponent i directly matches how many places in from the right that position is.
A fresh inner loop recomputes 26 to the power of i from nothing for every single position, with no memory of the power computed for the position right before it.
Each letter's contribution, its value times its positional weight, is added independently into the running total, mirroring the definition of a positional number system directly.

blocks.text: This is correct, since every letter is weighted by exactly the right power of 26 for its position, and all the weighted values are summed together.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), since computing 26 to the power of i from scratch takes O(i) time, and this is repeated for every one of the n positions.
Space: O(1) extra space.

Limitation: recomputing each power of 26 from nothing, every single time, repeats a huge amount of multiplication that was already implicitly done for the previous position. Reading the title from the other direction, left to right, lets each new letter be folded directly into a running result using just one multiplication and one addition, without ever computing a power explicitly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why recomputing each power works but is wasteful: 26 to the power of i is built completely from scratch for every position, even though the power for position i is just 26 times the power for position i minus 1.

What is the actual relationship between reading direction and the calculation: reading right to left forces you to know how far a digit is from the end before you can weight it, but reading left to right lets each digit be folded in immediately, since its correct weight is simply "everything read so far, shifted over by one base position".

Can this shift-and-add idea be reused from elsewhere: yes, it is exactly the same technique used to rebuild a number one digit at a time in Reverse Integer, just applied left to right here instead of digit by digit from a peeled value.

Does the missing zero digit change anything about this technique: no, since A is worth 1, adding the letter's value directly after shifting still produces the correct positional value, the technique itself does not depend on whether the smallest digit is 0 or 1.

The core idea: read the title left to right, and for every letter, multiply the running result by 26 and add the letter's value directly.

Read the title from left to right instead. Keep a running result, and for every new letter, first shift the existing result one place to the left in base 26, by multiplying it by 26, then add the new letter's value directly. This is the same idea used to read an ordinary base 10 number left to right, one digit at a time.
Read the title left to right, shifting the running result by the base and adding each new letter directly.

blocks.caption: Optimized flow: shift the result left in base 26 and add each new letter directly

codes.python:
def title_to_number(column_title):
    result = 0
    for ch in column_title:                       # read the title from left to right
        letter_value = ord(ch) - ord('A') + 1
        result = result * 26 + letter_value          # shift left in base 26, add this letter directly
    return result


if __name__ == "__main__":
    column_title = "ZY"
    print(title_to_number(column_title))

blocks.text: This works because a positional number is defined exactly this way, each digit already read so far represents a value that becomes one base position more significant the moment a new digit is appended, which is precisely what multiplying by 26 accomplishes; adding the new letter's value directly then places it correctly as the new least significant position. Since this reproduces the exact same weighted sum as the brute force definition, just computed incrementally, the two approaches always agree.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a genuine complexity class improvement, every letter is folded in with a single multiplication and addition.
Space: O(1) extra space, this is the real floor for this problem, since every letter must still be read at least once.

blocks.text: This is the classic pattern for evaluating any positional number system left to right, shift the running result by the base, then add the next digit, avoiding ever computing a power of the base explicitly. The exact same idea works for base 10, base 2, or, as here, a base 26 system that happens to have no zero digit.

items: Forgetting that A is worth 1, not 0, which is what makes this different from an ordinary base 26 positional system.
Recomputing a power of 26 from scratch for every position instead of folding letters in from left to right.
Mixing up which end of the string is the most significant position.

blocks.text: Naming this out loud as a base conversion problem, and explicitly noting that it lacks a zero digit compared to an ordinary positional system, shows a clear understanding of exactly why Excel columns count the way they do, past Z straight into AA.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid computing powers explicitly", think: read left to right, shift the running result by the base, add the new digit directly.
If the interviewer says "how is this different from an ordinary base conversion", think: this base has no digit worth zero, A already equals 1.
If the interviewer says "can you reverse this, converting a number back to a title", think: repeatedly take the value modulo 26, adjusting for the missing zero digit, then divide, similar in spirit to Reverse Integer's digit peeling.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The brute force approach recomputes each power of 26 from scratch, giving O(n squared) time and O(1) space. The left to right accumulation approach folds in each letter with a single multiply and add, giving O(n) time, a genuine complexity class improvement, with the same O(1) space.

items: Pattern: positional number system evaluation, reading digits left to right and folding each one in with a shift-and-add step, applied to a base 26 system that happens to have no zero digit.

Core Idea: read the title left to right, and for every letter, multiply the running result by 26 and add the letter's value directly, the same shift-and-add idea used to rebuild a number in Reverse Integer, just applied in a different base and a different reading direction.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized version.
Space: O(1) extra for both versions.
Most Important Observation: reading a positional number left to right lets every digit be folded in immediately with a shift and an add, with no need to ever compute an explicit power of the base.
Interview Difficulty: easy to write the brute force version; recognizing this as an ordinary base conversion with one missing digit is what shows real understanding.
One line memory trick: result equals result times 26 plus the letter's value, read left to right, no zero digit.
